Case A

A1. The seven-day search of the key's requests returned only the earlier requests from the one region, so nothing earlier was misuse. The key was published only 19 minutes before the burst, so a prior misuse can't be ruled out from a seven-day search that covers it. Still, the search showed only the stable-fingerprint requests. Within the search window, the burst was the first anomalous use. The answer is "No" only if something earlier was misuse, and nothing shown suggests that. The question asks whether the burst was the first misuse, and the evidence supports Yes: the earlier requests were the stable client and the search found nothing else. One caveat is that the earlier requests were in one region with a stable fingerprint, which fits the legitimate owner. I'll answer Yes.

A2. The check scored the account 30 minutes after publication, and the burst occurred at 19 minutes, so the burst was available to it. We don't know what inputs the check uses, so we can't say it missed evidence it had access to. Cannot tell.

A3. A shared payout destination alone doesn't establish a single owner. No, not by itself.

A4. Thirty days with no report or finding is weak at best, because absence of a record isn't evidence that nobody looked. The options are "Yes, weakly", "No" and "Cannot tell". The lack of any recorded finding doesn't show that anyone investigated, so I lean to Cannot tell.

A5. The burst involved a new fingerprint, a proxy, a payout change and a faster schedule shortly after publication. That warrants investigation. Yes.

Case B

B1. D has 0 chargebacks out of 100, against 2 for each of the others. Yes.

B2. A combined 5 percent is an aggregate, and it doesn't show that no individual account is above 5 percent. Also, the measure includes alerts, which aren't broken out per account. No.

B3. The search found no accounts beyond A and the closed account, but it covers only what the search can match. It might miss other names or entities. Cannot tell.

B4. Two notes from different analysts on different days may still rest on the same underlying evidence, and independence isn't shown. Cannot tell. They're separate authors, but nothing shows they reached their conclusions independently of each other. Cannot tell.

B5. A blocked payment never reached the chargeback stage, so the lack of a chargeback says nothing about whether it was fraud. No.

B6. The shared templates, descriptor pattern, and a person linked to A, a closed account and a rejected application justify a joint look. Yes.

RESULT MN-088 | A1: Yes | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: Yes | B2: No | B3: Cannot tell | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
